Title: What RAG Actually Changes
QuestionDetail: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, introduced in a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues, changes what about a model's answer?
AnswerDetails: The 2020 paper 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks' paired a retriever over an external corpus with a generator, so the answer draws on non-parametric memory - documents that can be looked up - alongside the parametric memory baked into the weights. Nothing is learned: the retrieved passages sit in the prompt for that one request and are gone afterwards. That is exactly why RAG is the standard answer to 'our content changes weekly'. You update the corpus, not the model, and the change is live on the next request rather than the next training run.
OptionA: It compresses the model so it runs on less hardware
OptionB: It permanently adds the retrieved documents to the model's weights
OptionC: It retrieves relevant passages at query time and puts them in the prompt, so the answer is conditioned on text the model can quote
OptionD: It makes the model refuse questions it cannot answer

Title: Why Keyword Search Still Earns Its Place
QuestionDetail: A vector-only retriever keeps missing documents when users search for exact product codes such as RX-4471. Adding BM25 keyword search alongside it fixes the problem. Why?
AnswerDetails: Embeddings place text in a space where similar MEANINGS sit close together - which is exactly what you want when 'how do I cancel' should match 'terminating your subscription', and exactly the wrong instrument for an identifier whose entire value is that it is a unique string with no semantic neighbours. Hybrid retrieval runs both and fuses the result lists, so semantic paraphrase and exact-token matching each cover the other's blind spot. Product codes, error numbers, legal citations, ticket IDs and proper names are the classic cases where the lexical half quietly saves the system.
OptionA: Embeddings capture meaning, so a rare exact token carries little semantic signal - lexical matching handles precisely what embeddings handle worst
OptionB: BM25 indexes more documents than a vector store can
OptionC: Vector search cannot represent numbers at all
OptionD: BM25 is faster than vector search

Title: The Chunking Trade-off
QuestionDetail: You are choosing a chunk size for your corpus. What is the real trade-off you are making?
AnswerDetails: Chunking is where most RAG quality is won or lost, and it is a genuine trade-off rather than a setting with a correct value. Too small, and you retrieve a sentence that no longer says what it is about - the 'it' whose antecedent was two paragraphs earlier, the figure with no units, the exception with no rule. Too large, and the embedding averages several topics together so the match gets muddier, while the passage eats context the answer needed. The usual escapes are structure-aware splitting on real section boundaries, overlapping windows, and stamping the document title and heading path onto every chunk.
OptionB: Chunk size affects indexing time only, not answer quality
OptionC: Small chunks cost more to store; large chunks cost less
OptionD: Small chunks match precisely but can sever a fact from the context that gives it meaning; large chunks keep context but dilute the match and consume the window

Title: Grounded and Still Wrong
QuestionDetail: Your system retrieves the correct passage and the model still answers incorrectly. Which diagnosis does that observation rule OUT?
AnswerDetails: If the correct passage was retrieved, then the corpus and the index are not the problem - and establishing that first matters, because 'add more documents' is the reflex fix and here it would achieve nothing at all. The remaining suspects all sit downstream of retrieval: ranking, where the right passage is present but buried under noise; context assembly, where it is truncated away before the model sees it; and instruction, where nothing in the prompt tells the model that the supplied text outranks what it believes it already knows. Splitting your evaluation into 'did we retrieve it' and 'did we use it' is what makes this distinction visible rather than argued about.
OptionA: The passage ranked below several irrelevant ones and was pushed out of the assembled context
OptionB: The retrieval index does not contain the answer at all
OptionC: The prompt never told the model to prefer the supplied passages over prior knowledge
OptionD: The model ignored the passage and answered from its own memory

Title: Citations as a Control
QuestionDetail: Requiring the model to cite the retrieved chunk behind each claim is valuable primarily because of what?
AnswerDetails: Citation does not stop a model being wrong; it makes being wrong DETECTABLE, which is a different and more achievable goal. Once every claim points at a specific retrieved passage, a reviewer can check it in seconds, and an automated grader can flag claims whose cited chunk does not actually support them - the failure usually called unsupported or unfaithful generation. That is a control rather than a cure, and it is one of the few that survives contact with a regulated review process, because it produces evidence somebody can inspect instead of assurance somebody has to trust.
OptionA: It prevents the model from generating any incorrect text
OptionB: It removes the need for an evaluation set
OptionD: It makes claims checkable - a reviewer or an automated grader can verify each statement against its cited source
